doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: Teaching swing through scatting triplets
summary: Duffy keeps the swing legacy alive and teaches students to swing by scatting triplets at any tempo.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I would like to kind of keep the legacy of the swing groove alive. You know there are a lot of the younger funk, rock drummers that are coming up trying to play more of the fusion jazz. But they don’t really understand the basic elements of just straight ahead swinging. You know, now you don’t really need a lot of education to know how to swing, you just have to let that ultimate feeling overtake your being. And then all of a sudden you latch on to a certain groove and you know you just start learning the vocabulary. It’s like people say well you can’t learn jazz, you know. But it’s all vocabulary you know. If you go [scats] then all of a sudden you’re understanding triplets and certain rhythmic feelings that will perpetuate the swing feel.
Do you have trouble teaching students to really swing? Is it a listening thing more?

Not really. I’ll tell you I have a little concept of thought where if I can teach you how to scat certain rhythmic and melodic figures — for example if you can say [scats] , and then take a little rest and take a breath, if you feel the triplets with certain accents, like [scats] if you can swing the triplets like that then you can fall right into the pocket of the groove, and then you’ll be able to swing at any tempo. Because you can go [scats] or [scats]. So whatever tempo, if you understand how to swing triplets, that will help you to swing.
That’s interesting because we’ll probably talk about swinging at a slow tempo in a few minutes.
